displayQuote: When a man is tired of London, he is tired of life

meta.title: Who really said "When a man is tired of London, he is tired of life"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Samuel Johnson really did say it — to Boswell on 20 Sept 1777. The famous half-line drops the rest: “for there is in London all that life can afford.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When a man is tired of London, he is tired of life'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Johnson — a spoken remark recorded by Boswell in 1777. See the full sentence the popular version cuts off.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: A genuine Johnson line — but a spoken one. He said it to James Boswell after breakfast on 20 September 1777, and Boswell recorded it in “The Life of Samuel Johnson” (1791). The famous fragment is the opening of a longer sentence: “when a man is tired of London, he is tired of life; for there is in London all that life can afford.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Life of Samuel Johnson, LL.D.

source.excerpt: “Why, Sir, you find no man, at all intellectual, who is willing to leave London. No, Sir, when a man is tired of London, he is tired of life; for there is in London all that life can afford.”
trail: Boswell records the line in The Life of Samuel Johnson ↗, where the full sentence continues “for there is in London all that life can afford.” The samueljohnson.com concordance dates the conversation to 20 September 1777.
Wikiquote lists it in its sourced section ↗, citing Boswell’s Life, Vol. III.
The samueljohnson.com concordance ↗ gives the same wording and the 1777 date.
source.excerptNote: Boswell had confessed he feared his love of London would fade if he lived there year-round instead of visiting; this was Johnson’s reply.
source.rightsNote: Boswell’s “The Life of Samuel Johnson” was first published in 1791 and Johnson’s spoken words were recorded then; both are long in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Samuel Johnson
author.heading: About Samuel Johnson
author.bio: Samuel Johnson — often “Dr Johnson” — was one of the most quoted figures in the English language, author of the landmark 1755 Dictionary of the English Language, poems, essays and the Lives of the Poets. Much of what we know of his talk survives because his friend James Boswell recorded their conversations, publishing them in the 1791 Life of Samuel Johnson. This London line is one of those spoken, not written, remarks.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Johnson is correct — a rare win for a “magnet” name. The distortions here are about form, not authorship.

items.why: The popular version stops at “tired of life” and drops Johnson’s reason: “for there is in London all that life can afford,” per Boswell ↗.
It is often presented as a Johnson epigram or essay line. It was a spoken reply in conversation, preserved only because Boswell wrote it down ↗ years later.

misattribution.truthLine: Johnson did say it — to Boswell on 20 September 1777 — and the real sentence runs on: “for there is in London all that life can afford ↗.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The remark came out of a real worry of Boswell’s. A Scot who lived in Edinburgh and only visited the capital, he feared that settling in London permanently would dull the thrill he felt on his periodic trips. Johnson’s answer was meant to reassure him that the city’s riches were inexhaustible.
Two and a half centuries later the line has become London’s unofficial motto — printed on mugs, tea towels and Tube posters — usually shorn of the clause that explains why Johnson believed it.
